doc.title: Bill Crow interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Reading, his mother's singing, and early love of writing
summary: Rowe asks if he was a player before a writer. Crow describes learning to read at home, his mother teaching him to sing, devouring the Kirkland library, and discovering the New Yorker and E.B. White.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: We are filming today for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive and it’s our great pleasure to have with us Bill Crow, who has multiple careers in music, as a bass player and a writer and working with the musicians, which is kind of first for us to be talking in that area, so it will be interesting to hear about how that work is going. Welcome, and I’d love to talk about some of your writing. First of all, can I guess that you were a player before you were a writer?

Yeah, well, I’ve always been interested in writing. I was a big reader when I was a kid, I learned to read before I started grade school. My mother had a little primer and she taught me at home. She also taught me to sing and I guess I inherited my musical ears from her. She was a musician. But I can remember standing by her ironing board singing songs with her before I could see up over the ironing board, so I know I was pretty young. And she tells me that when I still used to take naps in the afternoon in my little crib in the bedroom, when she would be teaching a singing student, she would sing the exercise she wanted them to sing, and then the student would sing it, and then they’d have to pause for me to sing it. But she got me started reading and I was omnivorous reader. I think while I was still in grade school in this small town outside Seattle, Washington — Kirkland, Washington is where I grew up, there was a small library operated by the ladies’ club. And the building is still there by the way. I was out there this summer and saw that it’s now a national landmark. But they had accumulated a nice little library of books for a small town, in the 20s and 30s. And before I was out of the fifth grade I’d read everything in that library. In fact when I got into Greek mythology I had to get a note from my mother — they wanted to make sure I wasn’t pressing flowers in these big books or something. But I read everything in the library it was fantastic. I’d take three or four books home a week and plow through them, you know? And so by the time I was in school I was always interested in English and composition and the teachers of those

things saw me as a prized student. So they fed me stuff. I think it was a sixth grade teacher that gave me copies of the New Yorker, which I’d never seen before. And I fell in love with James Thurber and E.B. White and Alexander Wolcott, and became quite a sophisticate for the small town that we were in. Some of the terms I didn’t understand at all, I had to go find out what they were talking about, but that was my beginning of my appreciation of really good writing. And I think E.B. White became my hero because he was such a master of the simple declarative sentence. He said what it was that he had on his mind without any question about what it was. He had a good sense of humor. And he was interested in things. Joseph Mitchell was another of my great heroes. He wrote articles about New York for the New Yorker and his stuff is now collected in a wonderful book. But unfortunately he hasn’t written anything. He’s still around but he hasn’t written anything for quite a while.
